culture-and-protocol.dress_and_conduct: Greet Aṉangu with 'palya'. Some find constant eye contact uncomfortable; silence usually means someone is thinking. Ask before photographing Aṉangu; commercial images need a permit.

laws.rule: A park pass is required to enter Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park. The official Parks Australia page lists an adult (18 years and over) pass at A$38 for 3 days or A$50 for an annual pass; children and teenagers under 18 go free. An annual pass for a Northern Territory-registered private vehicle (not a tour or hire vehicle) is A$109 and covers the driver and all passengers. The pass is for this park only; Kakadu needs a separate pass. You can buy it online or at the entry station. Commercial work, or a visit to Aboriginal land outside the park, may need an additional permit.

The Uluṟu climb has been closed permanently since 26 October 2019. Parks Australia says climbing Uluṟu is a breach of the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act and that penalties will be issued to visitors who attempt it. The park's Respecting Culture page also asks visitors to stay on marked tracks and paths and not to climb onto rock formations or boulders, so they do not enter sacred areas.

Parks Australia says culturally sensitive sites in the park must not be photographed: the rock details at those sites are treated as sacred scripture for Aṉangu and should only be viewed in their original location by the people entitled to see them. On the north-east face, Aṉangu ask photographers to take only wide shots from a distance and to avoid showing details on the top-left side of the rock; the page says the best time for that face is 1 to 2 hours before sunset, when shadows obscure the sacred sites. The Respecting Culture page also says: do not enter or photograph restricted areas, including sacred sites, ceremonial sites, burial grounds and people's homes; always ask permission before photographing Aṉangu; and a permit is required for commercial use of images of the park.
